tx.t: Let me tell you something about the history and the economics of coffee. According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder called Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became lively after eating the berries.

By the fifteenth century, coffee was grown in Yemen, and it then spread to Turkey and Europe. There are two main kinds of coffee, Arabica and Robusta, and about sixty per cent of the world's coffee is Arabica.
Brazil produces about one third of the world's coffee, more than any other country. People around the world drink about two billion cups of coffee every day.

tx.t: Researchers at Northfield College carried out a study in twenty twenty-three to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed one hundred and eleven students over five weeks.
On average, the students studied for seven hours a day. However, only thirty-nine per cent of them used any planned method.

The students who used the method of studying in short sessions with breaks remembered more of the material a week later. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.

tx.t: Today we are going to look at Antarctica, the coldest continent. About ninety-eight per cent of Antarctica is covered in ice.
The ice contains about seventy per cent of the world's fresh water. No people are native to Antarctica. Only scientists live there, and their numbers change with the seasons.
The Antarctic Treaty of nineteen fifty-nine, signed by twelve countries, says that the continent can be used only for peaceful purposes and science. Penguins, seals and whales live around its coasts.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Brenton. It began in twenty ten with five hundred and ninety-seven bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by seventy-seven per cent, and on a busy day there were more than thirty-seven thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: too few bikes in the hills. The council solved it with a van that moves bikes uphill every morning.
Today, a ride costs one pounds fifty-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: This week we are studying the life of Marie Curie, one of the most important scientists of the twentieth century. She was born in Warsaw in eighteen sixty-seven and moved to Paris to study when she was twenty-four.

Together with her husband Pierre, she discovered two new elements, polonium and radium, in eighteen ninety-eight. In nineteen oh three she won the Nobel Prize in Physics, becoming the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize.
In nineteen eleven she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry. During the First World War, she developed mobile X-ray units that doctors used to treat wounded soldiers.
She died in nineteen thirty-four, probably because of her long exposure to radiation.

tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

In nineteen seventy-one, Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers and chose the at sign for addresses. Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties.

The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it. Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University.
Today, more than five billion people use the internet.

By two thousand and six, the number had risen to four hundred and fifty-five pairs, which shows that careful management can work.
